claim: Voltage-gated proton (Hv) channels are standalone voltage sensors without separate ion conductive pores.
source: Voltage-gated proton (Hv) channels are standalone voltage sensors without separate ion conductive pores.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Hv channels, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Hv channels are gated by both voltage and transmembrane proton gradient (i.e., ∆pH).
source: They are gated by both voltage and transmembrane proton gradient (i.e., ∆pH), serving as acid extruders in most cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hv channel gating properties.

claim: Hv channels serve as acid extruders in most cells.
source: They are gated by both voltage and transmembrane proton gradient (i.e., ∆pH), serving as acid extruders in most cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physiological function of Hv channels.

claim: Hv channels are a bundle of four helices (named S1–S4), with the S4 segment carrying three positively charged Arg residues.
source: Like the canonical voltage sensors, Hv channels are a bundle of four helices (named S1 –S4), with the S4 segment carrying three positively charged Arg residues.
evidence: This structural information is established knowledge about Hv channels.

claim: The S4 segment moves outwards upon activating voltage in voltage-gated ion channels.
source: Extensive structural and electrophysiological studies on voltage-gated ion channels, in general, agree on an outwards movement of the S4 segment upon activating voltage, but the real-time conformational transitions are still unattainable.
evidence: This is established knowledge from extensive structural and electrophysiological studies.

claim: Real-time conformational transitions of voltage sensors are still unattainable.
source: Extensive structural and electrophysiological studies on voltage-gated ion channels, in general, agree on an outwards movement of the S4 segment upon activating voltage, but the real-time conformational transitions are still unattainable.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The study examined conformational dynamics of hHv1 channels using single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET).
source: With purified human voltage-gated proton (hHv1) channels reconstituted in liposomes, we have examined its conformational dynamics, including the S4 segment at different voltage and pHs using single-molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer (smFRET).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Both voltage and pH gradient shift the conformational dynamics of the S4 segment to control channel gating.
source: Here, we provide the first glimpse of real-time conformational trajectories of the hHv1 voltage sensor and show that both voltage and pH gradient shift the conformational dynamics of the S4 segment to control channel gating.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on smFRET data.

claim: The S4 segment transits among three major conformational states.
source: Our results indicate that the S4 segment transits among three major conformational states and only the transitions between the inward and outward conformations are highly dependent on voltage and pH.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on smFRET measurements and kinetic analysis.

claim: Only the transitions between the inward and outward conformations are highly dependent on voltage and pH.
source: Our results indicate that the S4 segment transits among three major conformational states and only the transitions between the inward and outward conformations are highly dependent on voltage and pH.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on kinetic analysis of smFRET data.

claim: Hv channels are solely composed of voltage sensors without the separate pore-forming domains typically found in canonical voltage-gated cation channels.
source: As a unique subfamily, voltage-gated proton (Hvs) channels are solely composed of voltage sensors without the separate pore-forming domains typically found in canonical voltage-gated cation channels (Ramsey et al., 2006; Sasaki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Hv channel voltage sensors are hourglass shaped with a bundle of four helices (named S1–S4).
source: Hv channel voltage sensors are hourglass shaped with a bundle of four helices (named S1–S4), like those of the voltage-gated cation channels (Takeshita et al., 2014; Bayrhuber et al., 2019).
evidence: This structural information is supported by cited structural studies.

claim: The S4 segment of voltage-gated cation channels is highly conserved and contains multiple positively charged residues to sense membrane voltage.
source: The S4 segment of the voltage-gated cation channels is highly conserved and contains multiple positively charged residues to sense membrane voltage (Gonzalez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: High resolution structures of voltage sensors largely agree on a model where the charge carrying S4 segment is driven outward by depolarization voltage.
source: High resolution structures of the voltage sensors from different organisms, including Hv channels, largely agree on a model where the charge carrying S4 segment is driven outward by depolarization voltage – a movement that is then transduced to gate the channel pore (Guo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from structural studies, supported by citation.

claim: Only the middle Arg in the S4 segment of the Hv channel switches its accessibility upon voltage activation according to accessibility assays.
source: For example, accessibility assays showed that only the middle Arg in the S4 segment of the Hv channel switches its accessibility upon voltage activation (Gonzalez et al., 2013), supported by the crystal structure of a voltage-sensitive phosphatase and the electron paramagnetic resonance data of the human Hv channel (hHv1) (Li et al., 2015; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by cited accessibility assays and structural studies.

claim: Gating currents of Hv channels suggest approximately three Arg residues move across the membrane barrier upon gating transition.
source: However, the gating currents of Hv channels and many other voltage-gated cation channels suggested approximately three Arg residues move across the membrane barrier upon gating transition (Carmona et al., 2018; De La Rosa and Ramsey, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited gating current studies.

claim: The voltage dependence of Hv channels is shifted by proton concentrations at the intra- and extracellular sides (i.e., transmembrane pH gradient).
source: Furthermore, a unique function-defining feature of Hv channels is that their voltage dependence is shifted by proton concentrations at the intra- and extracellular sides (i.e., transmembrane pH gradient) (Cherny et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Hv channels are only activated when the proton electrochemical gradient is directed outwards.
source: As a result, Hv channels are only activated when the proton electrochemical gradient is directed outwards (DeCoursey, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: H168 has been identified as a critical intracellular pH sensor in hHv1 channels.
source: Titratable residues were proposed to be involved in the pH regulation of Hv channels and H168 has been identified as a critical intracellular pH sensor in hHv1 channels (Cherny et al., 2015; Cherny et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both pH gradient and voltage alter the dynamics of the Hv channel gating currents that reflect the movements of the S4 segment.
source: In addition, the most recent studies indicated that both pH gradient and voltage alter the dynamics of the Hv channel gating currents that reflect the movements of the S4 segment (DeCoursey, 2018a; Carmona, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited recent studies.

claim: The codon-optimized hHv1 WT channels with an N-terminal 6× histidine tag were expressed and purified from E. coli host cells, exhibiting a single, symmetric peak in size-exclusion chromatography profile.
source: The codon-optimized hHv1 WT channels with an N-terminal 6× histidine tag were expressed and purified from E. coli host cells, exhibiting a single, symmetric peak in size-exclusion chromatography profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from protein purification, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The purified hHv1 WT protein retained its native proton channel function.
source: Our results indicated that the purified hHv1 WT protein retained its native proton channel function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from liposome flux assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The two intrinsic Cys107 and Cys249 residues were mutated into Ser for smFRET studies.
source: To implement smFRET studies on the hHv1 channel, we mutated the two intrinsic Cys107 and Cys249 residues into Ser, then introduced cysteine mutations, one pair at a time, at different sites of the hHv1 channel.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for smFRET studies.

claim: hHv1 channels in liposomes exist mainly as monomers because the concentration of hHv1 proteins during reconstitution is only 38 nM, while the dissociation constant of homodimeric hHv1 proteins is ~3.2 µM.
source: Moreover, hHv1 channels in liposomes exist mainly as monomers because the concentration of hHv1 proteins during reconstitution is only 38 nM, while the dissociation constant of homodimeric hHv1 proteins is ~3.2 µM (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the protein concentration used and the known dissociation constant from cited literature.

claim: The N214R mutation significantly reduces the outward H+ currents without altering the voltage dependence of hHv1 channels.
source: To circumvent this problem, we introduced the N214R mutation, which was shown to significantly reduce the outward H+ currents without altering the voltage dependence of hHv1 channels (Carmona et al., 2018; De La Rosa and Ramsey, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited studies.

claim: hHv1 N214R proteins reconstituted into liposomes exhibit no detectable proton uptake within 30 min.
source: We confirmed that hHv1 N214R proteins reconstituted into liposomes exhibit no detectable proton uptake within 30 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, upper left panel).
evidence: This is experimental data from liposome flux assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Most hHv1 proteins without the N214R mutation remained functional to mediate proton uptake despite multiple mutations and attached fluorophores.
source: Our liposome flux assay data indicated that, despite these modifications, most hHv1 proteins without the N214R mutation remained functional to mediate proton uptake (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is experimental data from liposome flux assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Substantial voltage-dependent FRET changes were detected at both the K169C-Q194C and K125C-S224C labeling sites on the N214R background.
source: On the N214R background, substantial voltage-dependent FRET changes were detected at both the K169C-Q194C and K125C-S224C labeling sites, which exhibited reverse FRET changes upon activating voltages (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: SmFRET traces from the K169-Q194 labeling sites exhibited large and spontaneous transitions among three major FRET states with centers at 0.24, 0.52, and 0.78.
source: SmFRET traces from the K169-Q194 labeling sites, exhibited large and spontaneous transitions among three major FRET states with centers at 0.24, 0.52, and 0.78, respectively, at both the resting (−85 mV) and activating voltages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The donor and acceptor fluorescence intensities were strongly anticorrelated, indicating that the FRET changes truly resulted from the structural changes rather than fluorophore photophysics.
source: For all these traces, the donor and acceptor fluorescence intensities were strongly anticorrelated, indicating that the FRET changes truly resulted from the structural changes rather than fluorophore photophysics (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The SSE (sum of squares due to errors) of Gaussian fits decreases >95% with three FRET states.
source: We fitted the histogram from the smFRET data collected at all voltages with one to five FRET states and the SSE (sum of squares due to errors) of Gaussian fits decreases >95% with three FRET states (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is data analysis result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Weak (0 mV) and strong activating (120 mV) voltages significantly enriched the low FRET-0.24 state at the K169C-Q194C sites, while diminishing the medium and high FRET state.
source: The FRET state occupancies calculated from several hundreds of hHv1 channels at different voltages showed that the weak (0 mV) and strong activating (120 mV) voltages significantly enriched the low FRET-0.24 state, while diminishing the medium and high FRET state (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Activating voltage altered the conformational distributions of the S4 segment by enriching those at the extracellular side.
source: Shifts of the FRET state occupancies indicated that activating voltage altered the conformational distributions of the S4 segment by enriching those at the extracellular side.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRET state occupancy data.

claim: SmFRET data from K125C-S224C sites exhibited large, spontaneous FRET transitions among 3 FRET states with centers at 0.27, 0.6 and 0.9.
source: The results were further validated by the smFRET data collected from the K125C-S224C sites (Figure 1A), which also exhibited large, spontaneous FRET transitions among 3 FRET states with centers at 0.27, 0.6 and 0.9 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Activating voltages (0 and 120 mV) promoted the high FRET 0.9 state at the K125CS224C labeling sites.
source: The activating voltages (0 and 120 mV), in sharp contrast, promoted the high FRET 0.9 state at the K125CS224C labeling sites (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Activating voltages promoted the transitions between the low FRET state at the K169C-Q194C sites and the high FRET state at the K125C-S224C sites.
source: The voltage-dependent changes in FRET state occupancies were also reflected in the transition density plots, which showed that activating voltages promoted the transitions between the low FRET state at the K169C-Q194C sites and the high FRET state at the K125C-S224C sites (Figure 1G, H).
evidence: This is experimental data from transition density plots shown in Figure 1G, H.

claim: The S4 segment of hHv1 undergoes spontaneous transitions at equilibrium state under all voltages.
source: Our smFRET data, from both the K169C-Q194C and K125CS224C labeling sites, consistently indicated that the S4 segment of hHv1 undergoes spontaneous transitions at equilibrium state under all voltages, and the activating voltage stabilizes the S4 segment at the extracellular side.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on smFRET data from multiple labeling sites.

claim: Activating voltage stabilizes the S4 segment at the extracellular side.
source: Our smFRET data, from both the K169C-Q194C and K125CS224C labeling sites, consistently indicated that the S4 segment of hHv1 undergoes spontaneous transitions at equilibrium state under all voltages, and the activating voltage stabilizes the S4 segment at the extracellular side.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on smFRET data from multiple labeling sites.

claim: FRET state occupancies of the S98C-Q194C sites demonstrated similar voltage-dependent changes as that of K169C-Q194C sites, although not statistically significant.
source: Among the labeling sites we examined, FRET state occupancies of the S98C-Q194C sites, which reflect the movement of S1 vs S4, demonstrated similar voltage-dependent changes as that of K169C-Q194C sites, although not statistically significant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: At Q194C-S219C (S4 itself), S98C-N132C (S1 vs S2), and K125C-K169C (S1 vs S3) sites, FRET state occupancies did not exhibit any significant shifts that could be potentially associated with voltage gating.
source: However, at all other sites including the Q194C-S219C (S4 itself), S98C-N132C (S1 vs S2), and K125C-K169C (S1 vs S3), FRET state occupancies did not exhibit any significant shifts that could be potentially associated with voltage gating (Figure 2).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Voltage primarily acts on the voltage-sensing S4 segment to promote its outward conformations.
source: These data suggested that voltage primarily acts on the voltage-sensing S4 segment to promote its outward conformations, while the S1, S2, and S3 segments probably do not undergo significant relative movements between each other during gating transition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFRET data from multiple labeling sites.

claim: The S1, S2, and S3 segments probably do not undergo significant relative movements between each other during gating transition.
source: These data suggested that voltage primarily acts on the voltage-sensing S4 segment to promote its outward conformations, while the S1, S2, and S3 segments probably do not undergo significant relative movements between each other during gating transition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFRET data from multiple labeling sites.

claim: The studies were performed on the hHv1 channels at equilibrium state.
source: Our studies were performed on the hHv1 channels at equilibrium state, as shown by the FRET contour maps, the FRET distributions did not change over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is confirmed by FRET contour maps shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The maximum open probability recorded from hHv1 channels in human eosinophils, even at the optimal pH gradient, is ~only 0.6.
source: A previous electrophysiological study indicated that the maximum open probability recorded from hHv1 channels in human eosinophils, even at the optimal pH gradient, is ~only 0.6 (Cherny et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge from a cited electrophysiological study.

claim: At 0 mV, lowering the intracellular pH to 6.5 remarkably enhanced the high FRET 0.9 state and decreased the low FRET 0.27 state occupancies at the K125C-S224C sites.
source: At 0 mV, lowering the intracellular pH (i.e., the extraliposomal pH) to 6.5 remarkably enhanced the high FRET 0.9 state and decreased the low FRET 0.27 state occupancies (Figure 3A, left).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At the K169C-Q194C labeling sites, lowering intracellular pH to 6.5 increased the low FRET state (F0.24) and decreased the high FRET state (F0.78).
source: Reverse changes in FRET occupancies were observed at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites, where the low FRET state (F0.24) increased and the high FRET state (F0.78) decreased upon intracellular pH 6.5 (Figure 3B, left panels).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lowering the intracellular pH enriches the outward conformations of the S4 segment.
source: FRET occupancy data from both labeling sites support that lowering the intracellular pH enriches the outward conformations of the S4 segment, consistent with its effect to shift the voltage dependence of hHv1 channels negatively, therefore promoting openings (Cherny et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an interpretation of FRET occupancy data, consistent with cited literature.

claim: Changing both the intra- and extracellular pHs symmetrically only shifted the FRET occupancies slightly.
source: In sharp contrast, changing both the intra- and extracellular pHs symmetrically only shifted the FRET occupancies slightly (Figure 3A, B, middle panels), agreeing well with the electrophysiological results that show the transmembrane pH gradient shifts the voltage dependence of hHv1 channels (Cherny et al., 1995).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 3A, B, consistent with cited electrophysiological results.

claim: The H168Q mutation attenuates the sensitivity of hHv1 channels to intracellular pH.
source: To further confirm our results, we introduced the H168Q background mutation, which was previously reported to attenuate the sensitivity of hHv1 channels to intracellular pH (Cherny et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: FRET distributions at both labeling sites no longer responded to intracellular pH changes on the H168Q background.
source: The results indicated that FRET distributions at both labeling sites no longer responded to intracellular pH changes (Figure 3A, B, right panels).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: pH gating of the hHv1 channels originates from its effect on the conformational dynamics of the S4 segment.
source: Our data showed that pH gating of the hHv1 channels originates from its effect on the conformational dynamics of the S4 segment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on smFRET data at different pH conditions.

claim: Voltage-dependent enrichments of the high FRET 0.9 state at the K125C-SS24C sites were almost abolished at intracellular pH 8.5.
source: Consistently, voltage-dependent enrichments of the high FRET 0.9 state at the K125C-SS24C sites were almost abolished (Figure 4A, right and middle panels).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The potential of activating voltage in enriching the low FRET 0.24 state was significantly attenuated at the K169C-Q194C sites at intracellular pH 8.5.
source: The potential of activating voltage in enriching the low FRET 0.24 state was also significantly attenuated at the K169C-Q194C sites (Figure 4B, right and middle panels).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The H168Q mutation enriched the high FRET 0.9 state at the K125C-S224C sites and the low FRET 0.24 state at the K169C labeling sites, at all intracellular pHs tested.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the H168Q mutation not only abolished the dependence of FRET distributions on intracellular pH but also enriched the high FRET 0.9 state at the K125C-S224C sites and the low FRET 0.24 state at the K169C labeling sites, at all intracellular pHs tested.
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The H168Q mutation may stabilize the outward conformations of the S4 segment.
source: These data propose that the H168Q mutation may stabilize the outward conformations of the S4 segment, therefore more negative voltage may be required to drive the S4 segment toward the resting state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFRET data from the H168Q mutant.

claim: The enrichment of the low FRET 0.27 populations correlating with channel closure was only observed on the K125C-S224C labeling sites at a more negative voltage (−200 mV) on the H168Q background, unlike those on the WT background that can be observed on the less negative voltage of −85 mV.
source: Indeed, we found that the enrichment of the low FRET 0.27 populations correlating with channel closure was only observed on the K125C-S224C labeling sites at a more negative voltage (−200 mV) on the H168Q background, unlike those on the WT background that can be observed on the less negative voltage of −85 mV (Figure 4A, left and right panels).
evidence: This is experimental data from smFRET measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The H168 residue may be involved in sensing intracellular pH through direct or indirect interactions with the S4 segment by stabilizing its inward resting conformations.
source: These data suggest that the H168 residue may be involved in sensing intracellular pH through direct or indirect interactions with the S4 segment by stabilizing its inward resting conformations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the smFRET data from the H168Q mutant.

claim: Only the transitions between the low and high FRET states (i.e., LH) exhibited voltage-dependent changes at both labeling sites under the same pH.
source: At both labeling sites, under the same pH, only the transitions between the low and high FRET states (i.e., LH) exhibited voltage-dependent changes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Activating voltage drove the equilibrium toward the high FRET state at the K125C-S224C sites and toward the low FRET state at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites.
source: Activating voltage drove the equilibrium toward the high FRET state at the K125C-S224C sites and toward the low FRET state at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At 0 mV and extracellular pH 7.5, only the equilibrium of the LH transitions was remarkably shifted by intracellular pH.
source: At 0 mV and extracellular pH 7.5, again only the equilibrium of the LH transitions was remarkably shifted by intracellular pH, lowering it to 6.5 enriched the high FRET state at the K125C-S224C sites and the low FRET state at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The H168Q mutation impaired the sensitivity of hHv1 channels to intracellular pH by diminishing the pH-dependent changes in Keq of LH transitions.
source: We further showed that the H168Q mutation impaired the sensitivity of hHv1 channels to intracellular pH by diminishing the pH-dependent changes in Keq of LH transitions.
evidence: This is kinetic analysis data.

claim: The S4 segment may transit among three positions across the membrane: the intracellular side (I), middle (M), and extracellular side (E).
source: Based on our smFRET data, the S4 segment may transit among three positions across the membrane, that is the intracellular side (I), middle (M), and extracellular side (E).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on smFRET data.

claim: The I conformation has two populations with their equilibrium depending on the protonation states of the intracellular pH sensor H168 and extracellular pH sensor that is yet to be identified.
source: The I conformation has two populations with their equilibrium depending on the protonation states of the intracellular pH sensor H168 and extracellular pH sensor that is yet to be identified (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is part of the proposed kinetic model shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Activating voltage mainly shifts the I–E transition by driving the S4 segment from the intracellular side (I conformation) directly to the extracellular side (E conformation), thereby promoting channel openings.
source: Activating voltage mainly shifts the I–E transition by driving the S4 segment from the intracellular side (I conformation) directly to the extracellular side (E conformation), thereby promoting channel openings.
evidence: This is part of the proposed kinetic model based on smFRET data.

claim: Both pH and voltage act on the S4 segment of the hHv1 voltage sensor to modulate channel gating.
source: In summary, our results suggest that both pH and voltage act on the S4 segment of the hHv1 voltage sensor to modulate channel gating, which is consistent with the most recent gating current recordings (Carmona, 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on smFRET data, consistent with cited gating current recordings.

claim: The mobilizing voltage of the S4 segment in hHv1 channels is probably much more negative, like those from canonical voltage-gated ion channels.
source: In hHv1 channels, the mobilizing voltage of the S4 segment is probably much more negative, like those from canonical voltage-gated ion channels.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with canonical voltage-gated ion channels.

claim: The pH sensors at the intra- (H168) and the extracellular sides may physically interact with the S4 segment, directly or indirectly, to stabilize it at the inward resting conformations.
source: However, the pH sensors at the intra- (H168) and the extracellular sides may physically interact with the S4 segment, directly or indirectly, to stabilize it at the inward resting conformations.
evidence: This is speculation based on the smFRET data and the proposed kinetic model.

claim: The molecular couplings between the S4 segment and pH sensors are dependent upon the protonation state of the H168 and other pH-sensing residues.
source: The molecular couplings between the S4 segment and pH sensors are dependent upon the protonation state of the H168 and other pH-sensing residues.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on smFRET data.

claim: The stability of the inward resting conformation (i.e., I) is tuned by pH gradient, which in turn shifts the equilibrium of LH transition that is driven by voltages to open or close hHv1 channels.
source: Thus, the stability of the inward resting conformation (i.e., I) is tuned by pH gradient, which in turn shifts the equilibrium of LH transition that is driven by voltages to open or close hHv1 channels.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on smFRET data.

claim: The S4 segment moves up for three helical turns in a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb.
source: For example, the S4 segment moves up for three helical turns in a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb (Wisedchaisri et al., 2019) while it moves up for only one helical turn in a voltage-sensitive phosphatase (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited structural studies.

claim: The S4 segment moves up for only one helical turn in a voltage-sensitive phosphatase.
source: For example, the S4 segment moves up for three helical turns in a voltage-gated sodium channel NavAb (Wisedchaisri et al., 2019) while it moves up for only one helical turn in a voltage-sensitive phosphatase (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited structural studies.

claim: Most atomic structures of voltage-gated ion channels were obtained at 0 mV voltage with their gating states unclear.
source: Unfortunately, most atomic structures of voltage-gated ion channels were obtained at 0 mV voltage with their gating states unclear, some even at the conformations that may not be physiologically relevant (Villalba-Galea et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a critique of existing structural studies, supported by citation.

claim: The spontaneous, large conformational transitions of the S4 segment in hHv1 channels are perhaps the structural basis of the gating current noise.
source: With smFRET imaging, we revealed the spontaneous, large conformational transitions of the S4 segment in hHv1 channels, which perhaps are the structural basis of the gating current noise (Sigg et al., 1994).
evidence: This is speculation based on smFRET data and cited gating current noise studies.

claim: The gating currents of Hv channels suggested multiple closed states.
source: The gating currents of Hv channels suggested multiple closed states (Carmona et al., 2018; DeCoursey, 2018b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited gating current studies.

claim: Long-time simulations have provided models of 'deactivated' and 'activated' conformations of hHv1 channels.
source: Although hHv1 channels at deactivated and activated states are NOT available, long-time simulations have provided models of 'deactivated' and 'activated' conformations (Geragotelis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited simulation studies.

claim: FPS software predicted the FRET changes from 0.28 to 0.57 at the K125C-S224C labeling sites from the 'deactivated' to 'activated' conformations.
source: From the 'deactivated' to 'activated' conformations, FPS software predicted the FRET changes from 0.28 to 0.57 at the K125C-S224C labeling sites, and from 0.72 to 0.45 at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites.
evidence: This is computational prediction using FPS software based on structural models.

claim: FPS software predicted the FRET changes from 0.72 to 0.45 at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites from the 'deactivated' to 'activated' conformations.
source: From the 'deactivated' to 'activated' conformations, FPS software predicted the FRET changes from 0.28 to 0.57 at the K125C-S224C labeling sites, and from 0.72 to 0.45 at the K169C-Q194C labeling sites.
evidence: This is computational prediction using FPS software based on structural models.

claim: The predicted FRET matched well with two of the three FRET centers identified by smFRET studies: 0.27 and 0.6 at the K125C-S224C sites, and 0.78 and 0.52 at the K169C-Q194C sites.
source: The predicted FRET matched well with two of the three FRET centers identified by our smFRET studies, that is 0.27 and 0.6 at the K125C-S224C sites, and 0.78 and 0.52 at the K169C-Q194C sites.
evidence: This is a comparison between computational predictions and experimental smFRET data.

claim: The simulation study perhaps did not reach the fully activated conformations.
source: Interestingly, the unmatched FRET 0.9 state of K125C-S224C and FRET 0.24 state of K169C-Q194C sites, represented the same activated conformation (i.e., the E conformation in Figure 5B). Our results imply that the simulation study perhaps did not reach the fully activated conformations.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison between smFRET data and simulation predictions.

claim: The oligomeric state of purified hHv1 channels is concentration dependent with an apparent dissociation constant of 3.2 µM.
source: A previous study by Li et al. showed that the oligomeric state of purified hHv1 channels is concentration dependent with an apparent dissociation constant of 3.2 µM (Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.
